questions.q: In the exact-case trace (θ = 1/4, n = 2), what is the measured outcome and its probability?
options: k = 1 (estimate 1/4), with probability exactly 1.000000
k = 2 (estimate 1/2), with probability 0.75
All four outcomes equally likely at 0.25 each
k = 0 (estimate 0), with probability 1.000000
questions.explain: Because θ = 1/4 lands exactly on the n=2 grid, the circuit is fully deterministic: P(k=1) = 1.000000 and all other outcomes have probability 0.

questions.q: In the non-exact trace (θ = 0.3, n = 3), what must be true of the 8 listed probabilities, and is it satisfied?
options: They must sum to 1, since measurement always yields exactly one of the 8 outcomes -- and the given values (0.021593 + 0.051768 + 0.577521 + 0.259336 + 0.040907 + 0.019440 + 0.014487 + 0.014948) do sum to 1
They must each individually equal exactly 0.125
Only the top two probabilities need to sum to 1; the rest are irrelevant
They must sum to 8, one unit of probability per outcome
questions.explain: Probabilities over all possible measurement outcomes must sum to 1; summing the eight given values confirms this holds.

questions.q: Why is k = 2 (estimate 0.25) the right outcome to report for θ = 0.3 at n = 3, even though it isn't exactly 0.3?
options: It is the single most probable outcome by a wide margin (57.75%, more than double the next-highest) and it is the nearest representable grid point to the true θ, which is the best any n=3 measurement can report
It is the only outcome with nonzero probability
It is simply the first outcome in numerical order
Because 0.25 and 0.3 are mathematically identical values
questions.explain: With only 8 discrete estimates available, the nearest grid point is the best possible single-outcome report, and k=2 is both nearest to 0.3 and by far the most probable result.

questions.q: According to the lesson's qualitative exercise, what is the only available lever to push the nearest-outcome probability for θ = 0.3 above 90%?
options: Increasing n (more counting qubits), which both shrinks the miss distance to the nearest grid point and reduces the failure probability ε per Lesson 12's formula, at the cost of needing larger powers of U
Changing θ to a different, more convenient value
Reducing n to simplify the circuit
Measuring the target register instead of the counting register
questions.explain: Lesson 12 established that more counting qubits sharpens the distribution around the nearest grid point, governed by the formula n = m + ceil(log2(2 + 1/(2ε))), at the cost of exponentially larger controlled-U powers.

questions.q: What does the relative size of P(k=3) = 0.259336 compared to P(k=4) through P(k=7) in the θ = 0.3 table suggest about the probability distribution's shape?
options: Probability falls off with distance from the true phase θ, so outcomes near the true value (even if not nearest) retain substantially more probability than outcomes far from it
Probability is distributed completely at random with no relationship to distance from θ
k = 3 is actually the nearest grid point, which is why it has higher probability
The distribution is flat, and all six remaining outcomes should have equal probability to k=3
questions.explain: k=3 is the second-nearest grid point to θ=0.3 and retains a large share of probability (25.93%), while outcomes further away (k=4 through k=7) each get much smaller shares -- consistent with probability concentrating near the true phase.
